value.overview: The Spot-fronted Swift (Cypseloides cherriei) is a small, poorly known swift of the tropical Americas. It is usually seen flying rapidly over forested mountains, foothills, and nearby open areas. Its dark plumage is relieved by distinctive pale spots around the eyes and bill, plus a variable whitish chin. The species has a scattered distribution from Costa Rica south through parts of Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Venezuela, and Peru, and is often difficult to study because it spends most of its life in the air.
value.classification: The Spot-fronted Swift belongs to the order Apodiformes and the swift family Apodidae. It is generally treated as a monotypic species, with no widely recognized subspecies.
value.identification: This swift is about 14 cm long, with a short, square-ended or slightly rounded tail and relatively short wings. The plumage is mostly dark brown to blackish, sometimes appearing browner in strong light. The most useful marks are a pale spot in front of the eye, a pale streak or spot behind the eye, and a variable white chin. Grayish underwings may be visible. Care is needed because fast flight and similar dark swifts can make field identification difficult.
value.rangeHabitat: The Spot-fronted Swift has a scattered range in the northern and western Andes and Central America. In Costa Rica, it is a rare and local species, recorded mainly along the Pacific-facing slopes of the Cordillera Central and Cordillera de Talamanca, including foothill and montane areas. It uses montane evergreen forest, tropical lowland evergreen forest, second-growth vegetation, and open airspace above forest. Records generally occur from about 700 to 2,200 meters, although lower elevations have also been reported elsewhere. Nesting sites are associated with wet cliffs and rock faces near streams or waterfalls.
value.migrationStatus: Its movements are poorly known. It is generally considered resident or at least present year-round across much of its range, but local elevational movements may occur. In Costa Rica, it is treated as a scarce resident or irregularly detected species rather than a confirmed long-distance migrant; seasonal patterns remain uncertain.
value.breeding: The species nests on vertical, damp rock surfaces, often beside or directly above flowing water. The nest is a small cup made from moss, ferns, and mud. A single egg is laid. Breeding records from the wider range span at least April through July, with timing varying by locality. In Costa Rica, available observations indicate nesting activity during the wet-season period, but the species remains insufficiently studied and its breeding distribution and colony sites are not fully documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Spot-fronted Swift is an aerial insectivore that captures small flying insects while in continuous flight. Recorded prey include true bugs and members of the bee, wasp, and ant group. It may forage alone or in flocks, and groups of up to several dozen birds can gather with other swift species over forest edges, valleys, and open slopes. Feeding activity is likely influenced by weather, insect abundance, and local airflow.
value.behavior: Like other Cypseloides swifts, it spends most of its time airborne and is usually observed as a fast-moving silhouette high over ridges, valleys, forest, or clearings. It may gather in mixed-species flocks while feeding. The species is not often seen perched, which contributes to the difficulty of confirming records. Its flight call is a rapid, high-pitched series of notes, but vocal information remains limited compared with better-known swifts.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is unknown. It has sometimes been described as apparently stable, but this conclusion is uncertain because the species is difficult to detect and has a scattered distribution.
